messages.content: You are a specialized Windows PowerShell automation assistant. Use powershell to query system state, manage processes, services, files, and configurations.
Wi-Fi adapter shows no connection and is listed as Disabled, check it and bring it up

<think>
A Disabled adapter explains no connection with no cable fault, since the interface is administratively down and cannot scan or associate. My plan is inspect then enable then verify to keep the change traceable. First I will run a read-only Get-NetAdapter for Wi-Fi to capture Name, InterfaceDescription, Status, LinkSpeed, and MediaConnectionState as baseline. Expected faulty state is Status Disabled with 0 bps and Disconnected media. This avoids touching the wrong adapter when multiple interfaces exist. No state change will be made in this first phase, only observation to prove cause before enabling.
</think>
Name: Wi-Fi, InterfaceDescription: Intel Wireless-AC 9560, Status: Disabled, LinkSpeed: 0 bps, MediaConnectionState: Disconnected, AdminStatus: Disabled
messages.name: powershell

messages.content:
<think>
Inspection confirms Wi-Fi with Intel Wireless-AC 9560 is Disabled at admin level, with 0 bps and Disconnected media, which fully explains the outage. The minimal safe fix is Enable-NetAdapter, which only flips AdminStatus to Enabled and lets the driver scan and associate using existing profiles. I will run Enable-NetAdapter with Confirm false to avoid an interactive prompt and keep automation clean. This does not alter SSID profiles, static addresses, or driver settings. Verification will follow with a fresh Get-NetAdapter to confirm Status Up and negotiated speed.
</think>
Adapter Wi-Fi enabled at 14:05:44. Status: Up, LinkSpeed: 866Mbps, MediaConnectionState: Connected.
messages.name: powershell

messages.content:
<think>
Enable reported success, so the driver should now scan, authenticate, and negotiate link speed with the known network. I need an independent verification because enable alone does not prove association or speed. I will run Get-NetAdapter for Wi-Fi and select Name, Status, and LinkSpeed to confirm operational state. Expected healthy result is Status Up with 866 Mbps and Connected media on this 802.11ac adapter. If Status stays Disabled or shows Not Present I will check driver state and hardware switch next. This closes the loop with measurable proof.
</think>
Name: Wi-Fi, Status: Up, LinkSpeed: 866 Mbps, MediaConnectionState: Connected
messages.name: powershell

messages.content: Wi-Fi adapter Intel Wireless-AC 9560 was Disabled with 0 bps and Disconnected media. Enabled it with Enable-NetAdapter and verified with Get-NetAdapter showing Status Up, LinkSpeed 866 Mbps, and Connected media. Connectivity should now work over existing profiles. If drops recur, check signal strength, roaming settings, and driver version in a follow-up.
